Design and motivation

Source: vignettes/articles/design.Rmd
design.Rmd

This article is for someone who wonders why R needs another regular expression package, or who wants to know what zuregex does behind a call before relying on it. It explains the reasons for the package and the choices in it. It teaches no function; for that, start with vignette("zuregex").

library(zuregex)

Why another PCRE2

Base R already matches with PCRE2 when you ask for perl = TRUE. So the pattern syntax is not the reason for zuregex. The reasons are in what base R does around the engine.

Base R with perl = TRUE zuregex
Compiles the pattern again on every call Compiles it once and keeps it in a cache
Matches on one thread Matches large inputs on several, where the build has OpenMP
Returns groups as attributes of regexpr() results, to take apart Returns them as character vectors and data frames, built in C
Replacement knows \\1 to \\9 PCRE2’s template language: names, groups past nine, defaults, conditionals, case forcing
No limit you can set on the work of a match Match, depth and heap limits per call
Uses the PCRE2 the platform has Bundles one version
Gives packages no way to PCRE2 from C A C API through LinkingTo

The last row is half the package. A package that needs PCRE2 in its C code has had to bundle its own copy, as vectorscan does. zuregex is PCRE2 packaged twice: as re_*() functions for R, and as a library for other packages, described in Link to zuregex from C.

One version on every platform

R takes PCRE2 from the system it was built on, so the version depends on the platform. zuregex compiles its own copy into the package, with every PCRE2 symbol hidden so that it cannot be confused with R’s. These are the two versions on the machine that built this page: the first is the same wherever zuregex is installed, the second is not.

zuregex_info()$pcre2_version
#> [1] "10.48"
extSoftVersion()[["PCRE"]]
#> [1] "10.42 2022-12-11"

Compiled once

Compiling a pattern, and JIT-compiling it, costs far more than matching one short string with it. A call inside lapply() or a Shiny reactive would pay that each time. So every pattern string goes through a cache of compiled patterns, keyed by the pattern, its flags and its other compile-time arguments, and the least recently used one is dropped when the cache is full. This is its capacity.

re_cache_size()
#> [1] 128

The size follows Python’s PyPcre. An re object from re_compile() holds its compiled pattern itself and stays valid whatever the cache does.

Several threads, one answer

A call does its work in three phases. The first reads the R strings, the second matches, and the third builds the R result. Only the second runs on several threads, with OpenMP, and it never touches R. That is what makes it safe, and it is also why results are identical for any number of threads: re_threads() is a performance control and nothing else.

A call whose subjects are small stays on one thread, because starting threads would cost more than it saves. zuregex_info() reports whether a build has OpenMP and where that threshold is.

What it was checked against

zuregex does not ask to be trusted on its own tests. Its results are compared with three other implementations:

  • PCRE2’s own test data, run through the C API.
  • Base R’s perl = TRUE and stringr, on a shared corpus, with every deliberate difference marked in the tests.
  • Python’s re, for splitting and the other behaviour taken from it.

Where the API comes from

The functions are new to R but not invented. The compiled pattern object and re_expand() follow Python’s pcre2.py. The flag letters and the JavaScript dialect follow node-pcre2. The grid of verbs, n to cap the number of matches, and re_escape() follow Go’s regexp package by way of go-re2.

What it leaves out

PCRE2 backtracks, so zuregex makes no promise of linear time; limits bound the work, as Bound the work of a match shows, and re2 gives the guarantee. The full list is under Scope in ?zuregex.

See also

Move from base R and stringr puts the differences from base R to use, function by function.
